decision.explanation: For x≠0, divide by x to obtain y'=6x^2. Integrating gives y=2x^3+C. Since y(-1)=2, -2+C=2, so C=4. This solution also satisfies the original equation at x=0.

after.name: Question 1
after.problem:
Find the particular solution to the differential equation below that satisfies the condition $y(-1)=2$
 

$$
x\cdot \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}=6{x}^{3}.
$$
after.worked_solution:
First, we rearrange the equation to give

$$
\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}=6{x}^{2}.
$$

Then, we integrate both sides with respect to $x,$ and get

$$
\begin{aligned}\int \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}\,\text{d}x & =\int 6{x}^{2}\,\text{d}x \\ y & =6(\frac{{x}^{3}}{3})\,\text{d}x \\  & =2{x}^{3}+C.\end{aligned}
$$

So our general solution is $y=2{x}^{3}+C.$ To find a particular solution, we substitute the condition $y(-1)=2$ into our solution and obtain a value for $C,$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}y & =2{x}^{3}+C \\ 2 & =2(-1)^{3}+C \\ 2 & =-2+C \\ C & =4.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, our particular solution is

$$
f(x)=2{x}^{3}+4.
$$

decision.explanation: Rearrange to y''=e^{3x}. Integrating twice gives y'=(1/3)e^{3x}+C and y=(1/9)e^{3x}+Cx+D. Differentiating twice verifies the equation.

after.name: Question 2
after.worked_solution:
First, we rearrange the equation to give

$$
\frac{{\text{d}}^{2}y}{\text{d}{x}^{2}}={e}^{3x}.
$$

Now, integrating the equation once, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\int \frac{{\text{d}}^{2}y}{\text{d}{x}^{2}}\,\text{d}x & =\int {e}^{3x}\,\text{d}x \\ \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =\frac{1}{3}{e}^{3x}+C.\end{aligned}
$$

Integrating a second time, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\int \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}\,\text{d}x & =\int (\frac{1}{3}{e}^{3x}+C)\text{d}x \\ y & =\frac{1}{3}\int {e}^{3x}\,\text{d}x+C\int \text{d}x \\  & =\frac{1}{3}(\frac{1}{3}\,{e}^{3x})+Cx+D \\  & =\frac{1}{9}{e}^{3x}+Cx+D.\end{aligned}
$$

Note that because we had a second-order equation, our general solution contains *two* arbitrary constants, $C$ and $D.$

Question 2
?

Solve the differential equation d2ydx2−e3x=0.

a
y=19e3x+Cx2+D
b
y=−19e3x+Cx2+D
c
y=13e3x+Cx+D
d
y=19e3x+Cx+D
e
y=−13e3x+Cx+D
Submit
Incorrect
EXPLANATION

First, we rearrange the equation to give d2ydx2=e3x.

Now, integrating the equation once, we get ∫d2ydx2dx=∫e3xdxdydx=13e3x+C.

Integrating a second time, we get ∫dydxdx=∫(13e3x+C)dxy=13∫e3xdx+C∫dx=13(13e3x)+Cx+D=19e3x+Cx+D.

Note that because we had a second-order equation, our general solution contains two arbitrary constants, C and D.

verification.explanation: The revealed solution confirms option d: integrating y''=e^{3x} twice gives y=(1/9)e^{3x}+Cx+D. Its second derivative is e^{3x}, as required. Option e instead has second derivative -3e^{3x}, so it is incorrect.

content.knowledge_point: Finding the General Solution of a Second Order Differential Equation by Integrating Twice
content.worked_solution:
First, we rearrange the equation to give

$$
\frac{{\text{d}}^{2}y}{\text{d}{x}^{2}}={e}^{3x}.
$$

Now, integrating the equation once, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\int \frac{{\text{d}}^{2}y}{\text{d}{x}^{2}}\,\text{d}x & =\int {e}^{3x}\,\text{d}x \\ \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =\frac{1}{3}{e}^{3x}+C.\end{aligned}
$$

Integrating a second time, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\int \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}\,\text{d}x & =\int (\frac{1}{3}{e}^{3x}+C)\text{d}x \\ y & =\frac{1}{3}\int {e}^{3x}\,\text{d}x+C\int \text{d}x \\  & =\frac{1}{3}(\frac{1}{3}\,{e}^{3x})+Cx+D \\  & =\frac{1}{9}{e}^{3x}+Cx+D.\end{aligned}
$$

Note that because we had a second-order equation, our general solution contains *two* arbitrary constants, $C$ and $D.$

after.worked_solution:
Integrating the equation once, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\int \frac{{\text{d}}^{2}y}{\text{d}{x}^{2}}\,\text{d}x & =8\int {e}^{-2x}\text{d}x \\ \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =8(-\frac{1}{2}{e}^{-2x})+C \\  & =-4{e}^{-2x}+C.\end{aligned}
$$

Integrating a second time, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\int \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}\,\text{d}x & =\int (-4{e}^{-2x}+C)\text{d}x \\ y & =-4(-\frac{1}{2}{e}^{-2x})+Cx+D \\  & =2{e}^{-2x}+Cx+D.\end{aligned}
$$

Note that because we had a second-order equation, our general solution contains *two* arbitrary constants, $C$ and $D.$
